nutshell: Tracking-by-detection MOT methods link objects across frames by thresholding Re-ID feature distances, but this paper shows the optimal threshold varies wildly from video to video (0.2 for one MOT17 sequence, 0.4 for another). It proposes computing a 'marginal probability' for each detection-track pair - a normalized distance derived by marginalizing over a small set of near-optimal assignment structures - which is far more stable across videos and lets one fixed threshold work everywhere.
contributions: A marginal-probability reformulation of data association: instead of raw Re-ID cosine distance, compute the probability a detection-track pair is matched by marginalizing over the space of possible one-to-one assignment structures, which the paper shows produces a much more stable distribution across different videos than raw feature distance.

An efficient approximation to make this tractable: rather than enumerating all n! possible matchings, iteratively compute a small set (n=100) of high-scoring, overlapping structures via L2-regularized MAP inference solved with the conditional-gradient/Frank-Wolfe algorithm (using the Hungarian algorithm as the per-step MAP subroutine), then marginalize only over that small set.

A drop-in replacement for the appearance-distance step in existing hierarchical (appearance -> motion -> IoU) matching pipelines, validated on top of both FairMOT and a Scaled-YOLOv4+BoT pipeline, yielding consistent ~1 point IDF1 gains on MOT17/MOT20 with negligible added inference cost (under ~20ms even on dense scenes) and improved robustness to occlusion.
deficiencies: The paper's own ablation (Table 2) shows the marginal-probability method has more ID switches than the simpler bi-directional softmax baseline (449 vs. 405) - the paper argues IDF1 matters more than ID switches, but doesn't demonstrate this tradeoff holds beyond the single ablation setting shown.

In the private-detection MOT17 benchmark (Table 4), MTracker's gains come with substantially more false positives (45,030) than several competitors like CenterTrack (18,489) or FairMOT (27,507) - a real cost of using a looser matching threshold (0.8 vs. the ~0.4-0.6 typical of distance-based methods) that isn't discussed as an explicit tradeoff in the results narrative.

The headline 'more robust to occlusion' claim (Sec 4.3) is demonstrated with exactly one qualitative example - a single occluded person across two frames of one MOT17-11 sequence (distance 0.753 vs. 0.725) - with no quantitative occlusion-specific breakdown (e.g. accuracy binned by occlusion duration) to support what's framed as a general property of the method.

The number of Frank-Wolfe/conditional-gradient steps (n=100), a core hyperparameter controlling the accuracy/cost tradeoff of the whole marginal-probability approximation, is fixed with no ablation showing how performance degrades with fewer or more steps.
notable: The core machinery - approximating an intractable marginal inference by finding a small set of high-scoring structures via L2-regularized MAP inference (SparseMAP-style, from Niculae et al., ICML 2018) - is a fairly elegant repurposing of an existing sparse structured-inference technique for a new application (calibrating raw feature distances into stable matching probabilities), rather than inventing new machinery from scratch.
